raw_text:
The objective of this study is to investigate and explain the persistent completion-time differences between sites employing the same nominal work process. The scope encompasses identifying measurable factors contributing to these differences and distinguishing between competing explanations through observable data.

Assumptions
- Differences in completion times are due to underlying factors rather than random variations.
- Measurable factors have an influence on completion times.
- Bayesian methods provide a framework capable of integrating prior beliefs with empirical evidence.

Research design
We will adopt a Bayesian observational study design, incorporating probabilistic models to quantify the uncertainty in estimates of the influence of various measurable factors on completion times.

Data or evidence needed
- Completion times for tasks at multiple sites using the same nominal work process.
- Measurements of relevant factors such as worker efficiency, resource availability, and environmental conditions at each site.

Measurement
- Completion time of tasks will be objectively measured using standardized timekeeping methods.
- Relevant factors will be quantitatively measured using surveys, observations, and automated recording devices where applicable.

Analysis
- We will model completion times as a function of the measurable factors using a Bayesian hierarchical model, incorporating prior beliefs about the relationships between factors and completion times.
- The model will allow for the variation in completion times across sites, with each site-specific model parameterized by observed data from that site.

Decision / stopping rule
- The study will continue until a stable set of factor measures that explains the majority of the variance in completion times is identified.
- The decision to stop will also consider practical constraints, such as resource limitations or predefined sample size criteria.

Limitations
- Assumes that the nominal work process is consistently followed across sites, which may not be the case.
- Potential for confounding variables that influence both the completion times and the measurable factors.
- Reliance on subjective prior beliefs in the Bayesian model may impact objectivity, though prior information can be as minimal as needed.
